video.titulo: Nepal Flood: The Warning System Built for the Wrong Disaster
video.descricao:
Sources: https://tinyurl.com/critical24
Emergency Preparedness Guide: https://payhip.com/b/GWENV

The Nepal flood that tore through Rasuwa on August 26 was published as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake, and then the USGS took the earthquake back.

At 8:37 in the morning local time, seismometers picked up something north of Kathmandu and the automatic solution went out as a quake. What actually happened was a rock and ice avalanche off Langtang Lirung, a 23,700-foot Himalayan peak, and the debris flow that followed ran down the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli valleys for nearly 100 kilometers. It took out 41 bridges, 26 miles of road, more than 300 vehicles, and a string of hydropower plants sitting on the same river.

CHAPTERS
0:00 The Earthquake the USGS Took Back
2:39 Langtang Lirung, the Mountain That Came Off
5:59 What the Water Passed Through in Rasuwa
7:30 The Instruments Reported a Magnitude 4.4
10:06 Zero Phases, Error 11.91, Status Reviewed
12:52 Long Period Waves and What Gave It Away
15:41 The Second Event Nobody Caught
16:56 The Warning System That Never Fired
18:39 Chamoli, Mount Rainier, and What to Actually Do

Have you ever watched an official number get revised after the fact? A magnitude, a damage estimate, a road that reopened later than they said it would. Leave the year and the town in the comments.

Subscribe to Critical Latitude for more on earthquakes, faults, glaciers, and what the planet is actually doing, with the science behind it.

SOURCES AND DISCLAIMER
Everything here comes from the published record: the two USGS event pages and the agency's own correction note, the USGS Landslide Hazards Program special event page, Dave Petley's Landslide Blog at Eos, the Ekstrom and Stark paper in Science, GFZ Helmholtz in Potsdam, the Shugar paper on Chamoli, and reporting from Nepal on the damage. Every link is at the top of this description. 

This video is educational. It is not a prediction that any specific mountain, glacier, or valley is about to fail.
